title: Confident lines, familiar object
objective: Use light searching marks and selected, deliberate lines to make a familiar object's shape clearer.

warmup.instructions: Draw a thumbnail-sized corner or outline of your book or key from life. Follow one edge three times—light, medium, then firm—and compare how pressure changes the mark.

explanation: Lines have different jobs: a light searching mark can help you locate an object's width, height, or direction, while a clearer stroke can record an edge you have checked. Start with light marks so you have room to adjust them as you look back at the book or key.

After comparing the large contour with the object, choose only a few lines to strengthen. A firmer or more direct line can clarify a corner, overlap, or turn; quieter edges can stay pale. Reuse Lesson 2's attention to observed contour, and let pressure or direction change only when it helps the familiar object read.

exercise.instructions:
1. Choose one familiar book or key and set it at a steady viewpoint. Keep it there for all three drawings. Spend two minutes noticing its overall proportions and the main turns in its contour.
2. In five minutes, make a small light-search drawing. Let a few marks overlap while you find the object's width, height, and direction; keep the lines pale.
3. In seven minutes, make a second small drawing. This time, select three lines that clarify the shape or an overlap; make those more definite and leave quieter edges light.
4. Spend sixteen minutes on a larger drawing. Start with light searching lines, compare the big contour with the object, then choose which lines to strengthen. Add a few identifying details, such as a key's bow and teeth or a book's cover and page edge.
5. Use the final two minutes to compare the three drawings. Notice which line choices made the object clearest. Soften stray searches only if they confuse the larger drawing; stop before shading.

reflection: Which line is clearest, and what changed in its direction or pressure?
Where did lighter marks give you room to adjust?
Did one edge need less emphasis than you expected?
extension: Make a second small drawing of the same object from another viewpoint. Keep the searching lines light, then choose one edge to emphasize.

teaching.whyItMatters: Choosing where a line is quiet or firm helps a simple drawing read clearly without tracing a dark border around everything.
teaching.connections: Lesson 2 asked you to follow observed edges instead of relying on a memorized outline. This lesson adds a choice about how strongly to record each line; the next framing lesson will use selected edges to make the relationship between objects easier to read.

deepDive: A searching line is useful because it keeps a decision provisional. Short, pale strokes can map the overall direction and allow small corrections while you compare the page with the object. Once a contour is checked, a longer or firmer stroke can make a useful edge easier to follow. Those marks are not separate stages for every artist, but they give a beginner a manageable way to notice the difference between looking for a shape and stating it.

Pressure is one way to organize attention, not a score for how finished a drawing is. A strong line can call out an overlap, corner, or turn; a light line can describe an edge that is uncertain or less important. If every boundary gets the same dark outline, an object may flatten into a symbol. Let what you see decide which edge needs emphasis, and leave enough light marks to revise a proportion when the drawing changes.

A darker contour works best when nearby marks give it room. Several equally heavy edges can merge corners and cover the quiet change between a cover and its page. Yet a light edge is not automatically unimportant; it can still describe an accurate change of plane. Decide from this view which few strokes need extra emphasis, then compare each study for clarity rather than neatness.

commonMistakes.mistake: Giving every edge the same dark, finished-looking outline.
commonMistakes.lookFor: All sides compete equally, search marks disappear, and the book or key reads as a flat symbol.

visual.alt: Two small book drawings compare an equally dark outline on every edge with a more useful mix of light search marks and a few checked firm edges.
visual.caption: A uniform dark border can flatten a familiar object.
